questions.q: Within the connective-tissue-disorder map, which disorder is marked most common and which is second most common?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis first; Sjogren syndrome second
Inflammatory muscle disease first; SLE second
questions.exp: The CTD map marks rheumatoid arthritis as most common and Sjogren syndrome as second most common. (Book p442)

questions.q: Which demographic profile is given for Sjogren syndrome?
opts: Women aged 40–60 years with F:M about 9:1
questions.exp: Sjogren syndrome is described as a multisystem autoimmune inflammatory CTD in middle-aged females (40–60) with F:M = 9:1. (Book p442)

questions.q: Secondary Sjogren syndrome is most strongly associated with which sequence of CTDs on the page?
opts: Inflammatory muscle disease more than RA
RA more than SLE more than inflammatory muscle disease
SLE more than RA more than systemic sclerosis
questions.exp: Secondary Sjogren has CTD association, ranked RA > SLE > IMD; primary has no such association. (Book p442)

questions.q: What proportion split is used for glandular and extraglandular Sjogren pathology?
questions.exp: Classification by pathology divides glandular (50%) and extraglandular (50%); extraglandular disease is multisystem and 15% is severe/life-threatening. (Book p442)

questions.q: What clinical hallmark is highlighted before the pathology section?
questions.exp: The clinical hallmark is dry eye and dry mouth; thyroid is noted as the simple endocrine organ involved and Sjogren can be an extrahepatic manifestation of HCV. (Book p442)

questions.q: Which is NOT listed among the page's extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis C virus?
questions.exp: HCV extrahepatic manifestations listed are cutaneous lichen planus, porphyria cutanea tarda, cryoglobulinaemia, Sjogren syndrome and MPGN. (Book p443)

questions.q: A patient develops dry eye, xerostomia, dry skin, dry throat and vaginal dryness after autoimmune lymphocytic exocrinopathy. Which process directly precedes these clinical symptoms in the page’s pathogenesis flow?
questions.exp: Genetic/environmental factors → autoantibodies → autoimmune lymphocytic exocrinopathy (periductal/perivascular) → ductal epithelial activation → the listed sicca symptoms. (Book p443)

questions.q: Which HLA association is stated for Sjogren syndrome?
questions.exp: Genetic factors list HLA-DR3; the note identifies SLE as another disease associated with HLA-DR3. (Book p443)

questions.q: Which helper-T-cell direction is drawn in Sjogren inflammation?
opts: Th1 greater than Th2, leading to B-cell involvement
Th2 greater than Th1 with absent B cells
Th17 only with no B-cell role
questions.exp: The inflammation line states T cell (Th1 > Th2) > B cell. (Book p443)

questions.q: Painless parotid enlargement in Sjogren is attributed to which cellular finding on the page?
questions.exp: IL-18-positive macrophages are linked to salivary-gland enlargement/painless parotid enlargement. (Book p443)

questions.q: A patient with anti-M3 muscarinic antibodies has troublesome dryness. Which pharmacologic class is linked to treatment in the source?
questions.exp: Antibodies list anti-M3 (muscarinic) → cholinergic agonist cevimeline for treatment, and anti-α-fodrin. (Book p443)

questions.q: Which salivary-gland biopsy is the gold standard in Sjogren syndrome?
questions.exp: Histopathology states minor salivary gland is gold standard and shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with T cells; major gland has benign lymphoepithelial lesions with B cells. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which immunohistochemical marker is shown with B-cell infiltration in the major salivary-gland panel?
questions.exp: The major-gland B-cell infiltration panel is labelled CD20; the T-cell infiltration panel is CD3. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which cellular pattern defines the minor-gland lesion of Sjogren in the source?
opts: Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with T cells
questions.exp: Minor salivary gland biopsy is gold standard and demonstrates focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with T-cell infiltration. (Book p444)

questions.q: A patient describes a gritty, sandy eye sensation and glare. Which mechanism is named in the dry-eye section?
questions.exp: Dry eyes are non-specific and may result from aqueous plus lipid/meibomian-gland dysfunction, producing irritation, gritty/sandy sensation and glare. (Book p444)

questions.q: What Schirmer-test result is used for dry eye on the page?
questions.exp: Dry-eye diagnosis: Schirmer <5 mm after 5 min; tear-film breakup time <10 s; ocular staining may use lissamine green or fluorescein. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which tear-film breakup time is marked abnormal for dry eye?
questions.exp: The source marks tear-film breakup time <10 seconds as dry eye. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts dry mouth with dry eyes in the clinical-features block?
questions.exp: The source calls dry eyes non-specific and dry mouth more specific. (Book p444)

questions.q: A patient must drink water to swallow, has chewing difficulty and dental caries. Which Sjogren manifestation is most directly illustrated?
questions.exp: Dry mouth manifestations: unable to swallow without water, chewing difficulty and dental caries. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which oral feature is listed alongside altered taste in Sjogren dry-mouth manifestations?
questions.exp: Continuation lists oral thrush, altered taste, and 25% salivary-gland swelling. (Book p445)

questions.q: About what proportion of Sjogren patients have salivary-gland swelling according to the page?
questions.exp: The source gives 25% salivary-gland swelling, usually bilateral painless symmetric. (Book p445)

questions.q: A child has recurrent episodes of acute parotitis due to duct blockade. Which source diagnosis context does this support?
questions.exp: Childhood Sjogren is described as recurrent acute parotitis due to duct blockage. (Book p445)

questions.q: A Sjogren patient develops asymmetric painful nodular parotid swelling with palpable nodes. What complication must be suspected?
opts: B-cell lymphoma of extranodal marginal-zone type
questions.exp: Asymmetric painful swelling with palpable nodules signals B-cell lymphoma (extranodal marginal-zone B-cell lymphoma), associated with cryoglobulinaemia and low C3/C4. (Book p445)

questions.q: Which laboratory pattern predicts extraglandular Sjogren on the page?
opts: Low C3/C4, anti-Ro/La, positive rheumatoid factor and cryoglobulins
questions.exp: Predictors listed: low complement (C3/C4), anti-Ro/La (SS-A/SS-B), positive RF and cryoglobulins. (Book p445)

questions.q: A diagnosed Sjogren patient has high anti-Ro/La titres and early onset/long duration. What prognostic association is stated?
opts: Extraglandular disease, poorer prognosis, B-cell lymphoma risk and salivary enlargement
questions.exp: Positive anti-Ro/La in diagnosed Sjogren indicates extraglandular disease, poorer prognosis, B-cell lymphoma risk and salivary-gland enlargement; ~5% may develop disease after 10–15 years. (Book p445)

questions.q: Jaccoud arthropathy in Sjogren is characterised as:
questions.exp: Manifestations include fatigue and arthralgia/arthritis with non-erosive Jaccoud arthropathy. (Book p445)

questions.q: A Sjogren patient develops dorsal-root-ganglion involvement with truncal ataxia. Which severe-system category is implicated?
questions.exp: Severe manifestations (15%) include CNS ganglionopathy from dorsal-root-ganglion involvement, causing truncal ataxia. (Book p446)

questions.q: What is the most common interstitial lung pattern listed in Sjogren?
questions.exp: Lung: risk ILD; most common NSIP. Most characteristic is lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP) with GGO, cysts and nodules. (Book p446)

questions.q: HRCT in Sjogren shows ground-glass opacity, cysts and nodules. Which lung disorder is described as most characteristic?
questions.exp: LIP is marked most characteristic and has GGO, cyst and nodules. (Book p446)

questions.q: Which renal manifestation is specifically attributed to tubulointerstitial kidney disease in Sjogren?
questions.exp: Renal: tubulointerstitial kidney disease causes distal RTA and has minor CKD risk. (Book p446)

questions.q: A patient reports Raynaud phenomenon that preceded sicca symptoms. Which additional warning is provided on the page?
opts: It is restricted to the first week of disease
It may produce critical limb ischaemia
It proves an absence of vasculitis
questions.exp: Raynaud may precede sicca in one-third and may produce critical limb ischaemia. (Book p446)

questions.q: What is the hallmark lesion of the most common vascular complication in Sjogren?
questions.exp: Small-vessel vasculitis is most common and hallmark lesion is palpable purpura. Medium-vessel disease is severe, with ulcers/gangrene, MPGN and neuropathy. (Book p446)

questions.q: A Sjogren patient develops ulceration, gangrene, MPGN and neuropathy. Which vascular category is indicated?
questions.exp: The source describes severe medium-vessel vasculitis with ulcer/gangrene and association with MPGN and neuropathy. (Book p446)

questions.q: Which combination supports concern for B-cell lymphoma in Sjogren?
opts: Persistent asymmetric painful nodular parotid enlargement with lymphadenopathy
High saliva flow with normal nodes
questions.exp: Lymphadenopathy prompts exclusion of lymphoma; indicators include persistent asymmetric painful nodular parotid enlargement with nodes, cryoglobulinaemia, low C3/C4, high Ro/La, purpura and leukopenia. (Book p446)

questions.q: Which disorders are associated with lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis according to the note?
questions.exp: Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis is associated with Sjogren and HIV. (Book p447)

questions.q: Which trio of disorders is listed as causing lung cysts?
questions.exp: Cysts in lung: LIP, Langerhans-cell histiocytosis and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. (Book p447)

questions.q: How often is ANA positive in Sjogren according to the investigation section?
questions.exp: ANA is a CTD screening test and is positive in 85% with Sjogren; if positive, ANA profile can detect anti-Ro/La. (Book p447)

questions.q: Which antibody has no independent diagnostic value in the source despite being positive in roughly one-third?
questions.exp: Anti-Ro is positive in 50%; anti-La has no independent value despite 33% positivity. (Book p447)

questions.q: ANA IIF shows fine-speckled pattern with negative metaphase cells. What does the source say this pattern suggests?
questions.exp: Fine speckled is most common, metaphase cells negative, and suggests anti-Ro/La/Sjogren. Dense fine speckled has DFS-positive metaphase cells and rules out CTD. (Book p447)

questions.q: Which test is called the investigation of choice/gold standard for Sjogren in this section?
questions.exp: Minor salivary gland biopsy is IOC/gold standard and shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (T cell). (Book p447)

questions.q: What unstimulated salivary flow is given as abnormal in the (now less-used) sialography note?
questions.exp: Sialography note: unstimulated salivary flow rate <1.5 mL/15 min; it is marked ‘not done now.’ Ultrasound shows loss of gland homogeneity. (Book p447)

questions.q: In 2016 ACR/EULAR classification, which two findings each carry three points?
opts: Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis focus score ≥1/mm² and anti-Ro/SS-A positivity
Schirmer ≤5 mm and low salivary flow
Ocular staining and Rose Bengal score
questions.exp: Score 3: histopathology focus score ≥1/mm² and anti-Ro/SS-A. Score 1: ocular staining/Rose Bengal, Schirmer ≤5 mm/5 min, and salivary flow <0.1 mL/min. (Book p448)

questions.q: What total is required for primary-Sjogren classification after at least one oral/ocular dryness symptom?
questions.exp: Rules: at least one symptom of ocular/oral dryness plus total score ≥4. (Book p448)

questions.q: Which condition is NOT in the printed exclusion list for Sjogren classification?
questions.exp: Exclusions include prior head/neck radiation, active HCV, AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, GVHD and IgG4-related disease. (Book p448)

questions.q: A pregnant woman with high anti-Ro/La titres is counselled about which fetal risk stated in the note?
opts: Tetralogy of Fallot in all pregnancies
questions.exp: High anti-Ro/La in pregnancy increases congenital heart block risk (2–5%). The source contrasts offspring risk for CTD in Sjogren male versus SLE female contexts. (Book p448)

questions.q: Which salivary-gland-enlargement differential pairs IgG4-related disease with the correct pathology/association?
opts: Storiform fibrosis, plasmacytic infiltrate and pancreatitis
Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with dry eyes
questions.exp: Differential: sarcoidosis = ILD + uveitis + hilar adenopathy; IgG4-RD = storiform fibrosis + plasmacytic infiltrate + pancreatitis. (Book p448)

questions.q: Which treatment is assigned to severe life-threatening extraglandular Sjogren manifestations?
opts: High-dose steroid plus immunosuppressant such as mycophenolate mofetil
questions.exp: Treatment: glandular saliva substitute/cevimeline/artificial tears. Fatigue/arthralgia uses low-dose steroid <7.5 mg/day + NSAIDs + HCQ; severe life-threatening disease uses high-dose steroid + immunosuppressant/MMF. (Book p448)

units.title: 1. Classification, Association & Pathogenesis
units.guide:
Sjogren syndrome is placed in the connective-tissue-disorder framework.
Primary/secondary and glandular/extraglandular classification are kept separate.
The HCV association and lymphocytic exocrinopathy mechanism lead into pathology.

units.title: 2. Histology & Glandular Clinical Features
units.guide:
Minor-gland pathology is distinguished from major-gland lesions.
Sicca symptoms are converted into diagnostic thresholds and patient presentations.
Parotid warning signs are kept distinct from routine painless enlargement.

units.title: 3. Extraglandular Disease, Investigations & Classification
units.guide:
Severe neurological, pulmonary, hepatobiliary, renal and vascular disease follows in printed order.
Tests and ANA patterns are interpreted before formal classification scoring.
Exclusions, pregnancy counselling, and source-directed treatment conclude the chapter.
